answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, 94% committed volume with no buffer, and an 18% spend cut. Only one decision fits this cycle, so it must deliver cost relief without touching physical supply continuity. memory_c4 (renegotiation with market benchmarking recovered price and payment terms) and memory_c6 (multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope) point to a negotiated renewal as the one lever that attacks TCO while the incumbent keeps shipping. I want the archived source for memory_c4 because it is the direct basis for my intended action and I need to know how much margin it actually recovered and whether that magnitude is anywhere near 18% \, if it was 3-4%, negotiation alone will not satisfy finance and I need to know that before committing. I want memory_c2 because switching to the low-cost vendor is the only inherited path with a documented sharp unit-cost cut, and it is the option I am rejecting; I need to see whether that 'quick onboarding' happened with slack in the line or under a buffer, since a switch executed at 94% utilization in 14 days is a different risk than what that record likely describes. memory_c1 and memory_c3 inform the shape of the risk (stability from incumbency; second-sourcing as the eventual fix for single-point-of-failure) but neither addresses the cost mandate this cycle; memory_c5's deferral is unavailable because this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means an actual supply gap. Downstream risk I am flagging explicitly: an 18% cut extracted purely through price pressure can be recovered by the supplier through quieter degradation \, lead-time slippage, lower inspection rigor, substituted subcomponents \, none of which appear in these memories because the memories record outcomes that were noticed, not the ones that were not measured. Any negotiated deal should hold service scope, lead time, and quality specs constant in writing rather than trading them invisibly for headline price. Residual uncertainty is real: none of these records carry the failure cases, all are archived summaries whose original context I have not yet seen, and the second-source gap flagged by memory_c3 remains open on the primary line and should be the next cycle's decision. If verification shows negotiation historically yielded only single-digit relief, the honest answer to finance is a partial cut plus a documented shortfall, not a rushed vendor switch into a line with no buffer.
